Before the first dawn, the world was a silent bowl of black water. In its center floated a single seed, silver as moonlight, guarded by an old turtle named Maru. For a thousand years Maru circled the seed, whispering stories to keep it warm.

One day the seed cracked, and from it sprang a tree whose roots drank darkness and whose branches pierced the sky. On the highest branch perched a golden bird. When the bird opened its beak, the first song poured out. The song became wind, the wind became clouds, and the clouds wept rain upon the endless sea.

Where each raindrop fell, land rose: mountains like sleeping giants, valleys like cupped hands, forests like green fire. But the world was still dim, so Maru climbed the tree and asked the bird for light.

The bird plucked one feather from its breast and cast it eastward. It became the sun. Another feather, softer and pale, became the moon. Tiny sparks shaken from its wings became stars.

Since then, turtles carry the memory of the dark waters, birds greet each dawn with song, and every seed dreams of making a world.

Before the moon learned to shine, the nights were sealed in a black jar kept beneath the roots of the oldest cedar. In those days, people slept early and dreamed only of footsteps, for no one could see the faces of their loved ones after sunset.

A small fox named Luma hated this. She loved stories, and stories needed eyes that sparkled. So she crept beneath the cedar and found the jar guarded by a stone serpent.

“Why do you keep the night so dark?” asked Luma.

“Because light makes shadows,” hissed the serpent. “And shadows frighten the world.”

Luma thought for a moment. “Then give me one drop. I will teach shadows to dance.”

The serpent laughed so hard its stone scales cracked. Through the crack slipped a silver drop. Luma caught it in her tail and raced up the tallest hill. She flung the drop into the sky, where it became the moon.

That night, every shadow stretched and bowed. Children laughed, elders remembered songs, and travelers found their roads.

The serpent, hearing joy instead of fear, opened the jar a little more. Its spilled sparks became the stars.

And foxes still carry white-tipped tails, in memory of Luma’s stolen moonfire.

Myth: Before lanterns and hearths, the world folded itself into a cloak of endless night. Beneath the roots of the first cedar, a clay jar held every glimmer that had not yet been born. Beside it coiled a serpent of river-stone, whose eyes had never blinked.

A young fox named Luma wandered the dark paths, listening to people speak without seeing their smiles. She missed the colors of berries, the silver of rain, the red paws of morning. So she slipped under the cedar and bowed to the serpent.

“Keeper, why do you hide the light?”

“Because light reveals sorrow as well as joy,” the serpent replied. “Better that the world remain unseen.”

Luma shook her white-tipped tail. “A hidden sorrow cannot be healed.”

The serpent considered this, and one stony tear fell upon the jar. It cracked. Luma caught the first silver flame and carried it up the mountain, where she set it gently in the sky. It became the moon.

Under its glow, people saw wounds, yes, but also hands reaching to mend them. The serpent opened the jar, scattering sparks into stars.

At dawn, one golden ember rolled east and became the sun. Since then, foxes run at twilight, guiding light between fear and hope.

Myth: Before rivers remembered how to run, the earth lay curled beneath a blanket of mist. In the hollow of a great stone slept Maru, the ancient turtle, carrying on his shell a garden of unawakened seeds. Each night he dreamed of a tree tall enough to touch what waited beyond the clouds.

At last one seed stirred. Maru pressed it into the mud and hummed the oldest song he knew. The seed opened, sending roots deep into silence and branches high into the gray. At its crown bloomed a blue flower, and inside the flower slept a tiny bird with copper wings.

When the bird woke, it shook itself, and music fell like rain. The notes struck the ground and became streams, then rivers, then seas. Fish flashed into being wherever the music pooled. Reeds rose along the banks and whispered the song onward.

Still, the mist hid every path. So Maru asked the bird to lift the veil. The bird gave one copper feather to the east, and it became sunrise. Another drifted west and became sunset. The mist blushed, thinned, and vanished.

That is why rivers sing over stones, turtles dream slowly, and morning always arrives on wings.

Myth: Before paths learned to lead home, the world drifted beneath a pale mist. In the shell of Maru, the first turtle, slept seven seeds, each dreaming a different color. Maru crawled for ages across the quiet mud, humming so the seeds would not forget becoming.

One morning, a green seed woke and pushed a root through his shell into the earth. From it rose a tree with leaves like small hands. At the top opened a lantern-flower, and inside stood a copper bird, shivering with unsung rain.

“Sing,” Maru whispered, “for the world is thirsty.”

The bird sang. Its notes fell into furrows and became rivers; its trills filled hollows and became lakes. Wherever water shone, creatures lifted their faces, but still they wandered, unable to see one another clearly.

So Maru offered the bird a blue seed. The bird cracked it gently. One half flew east and burned into dawn; the other floated west and softened into dusk. Between them the mist opened like a curtain.

Since then, turtles carry gardens patiently, birds call rain from silence, and every road remembers the first light that taught travelers to recognize each other's eyes and share their bread beneath branches.

Moved, the serpent broke the jar. Sparks streamed upward as stars, while one warm ember rolled east and became sunrise.

Since then, foxes wear pale tail-tips, serpents bask in morning, and light returns because courage once entered the roots.

Since then, turtles guard patient gardens, birds keep rain in their songs, and no stranger is refused water.
